title: Not Nvidia. Not Microsoft. This "Magnificent Seven" Stock Is the Cheapest Right Now.

As the old adage goes, you get what you pay for. In other words, if you want quality, you can expect to pay a premium for it. The idea applies within the world of investing as well.

Still, knowing that stocks' prices and valuations constantly ebb and flow -- sometimes to extremes -- it's not wrong to think about the price you're paying to plug into a particular company's performance.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

This premise presents a potential opportunity to investors interested in the market's biggest and highest-profile names. Although they're all so-called "Magnificent Seven" stocks, one of these names is measurably cheaper than all the others right now. While not a reason in and of itself to step in, this valuation bolsters the existing bullish case.

This Mag-7 bargain? Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), priced at just over 16 times this year's analyst-projected per-share earnings of $20.59.

The numbers

If you've been keeping tabs on Google's parent company and its recent quarter, you already know something important. Its earnings projection includes a $6.26-per-share second-quarter accounting benefit linked to the growth of the company's investments in SpaceX and Anthropic. Without that one-time bump, Alphabet's only on track to earn $14.33 per share this year, translating into a price-to-earnings ratio of a little more than 23.

That's not exactly cheap, but it's not outrageous either. It's less than Nvidia's 2026 comparison of 24, as well as Microsoft's P/E ratio of 27 based on this year's expected earnings of $19.76 per share. Indeed, the only Magnificent Seven name that's even sort of close is Amazon. However, like Alphabet, it too reported a big gain from its stake in Anthropic during Q2 of this year. Indeed, $53.4 billion of its Q2 $62.6 billion in net income came from its Anthropic holding. Strip that out, and Amazon stock is valued at roughly 27 times 2026's anticipated profit.

There's more than one way to value a stock, of course. Arguably the more meaningful way is based on that company's future earnings. That's where things start changing a bit here.

title: If I Could Only Own 1 ETF for the Next 20 Years, Here's Exactly What I'd Pick and Why

If I Could Only Own 1 ETF for the Next 20 Years, Here's Exactly What I'd Pick and Why

Sun, October 25, 2026 at 10:22 AM PDT 4 min read

VGT

Trading disclosure

If tomorrow you had to sell off all of your exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and just invest in one lone ETF for the next 20 years, which one would it be?

For me, it would be the Vanguard Information Technology ETF (NYSEMKT: VGT).

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

My thought process is that, for a 20-year period or more, I want an aggressive growth fund, because history has shown that over long periods, many aggressive growth funds outperform the market and other investment styles, like value or income. Over a longer investment horizon, the fund has more time for its growth to compound and navigate the inevitable, sometimes volatile, ups and downs.

Also, I want to invest in a sector that has been driving the market for the past 40 years or more, and will probably continue to do so for decades to come: technology.

Image source: Getty Images.

There are, of course, many technology-focused ETFs, but I would select the Vanguard Information Technology ETF as my one ETF for a few specific reasons.

Why the Vanguard Information Technology ETF

Among all of the major technology-centric ETFs on the market, the Vanguard Information Technology ETF casts the widest net. It holds roughly 318 technology stocks, which is more than just about all tech ETFs.

I like that diversification within the sector, which we all know can be volatile. It tracks the MSCI US Investable Market Information Technology 25/50 Index, an index of large, medium, and small U.S. companies in the information technology sector.

It is generally made up of internet services and infrastructure companies, which include data centers, cloud networking, and storage infrastructure. It also encompasses information technology consulting and services companies, hardware and equipment companies, and semiconductor manufacturers.

Again, it is a sector fund, so it is inherently riskier than more diversified funds, but among tech ETFs, it includes a broader mix of tech stocks of different sizes and from different areas of the sector.

Best-in-class performance

Over the past 20 years, the Vanguard Information Technology ETF has been the best performer among tech ETFs with a similar track record.

It is very close, as the chart below shows, but the VGT ETF has averaged a 17% average annualized return over the past 20 years. In addition, it has a very low expense ratio of 0.09%.

title: 3 Superior Growth Stocks to Buy Now and Hold for 10 Years

Building wealth over a decade often comes down to owning companies that ride a long-lasting trend, and artificial intelligence (AI) spending is one of the biggest. Research firm Gartner expects worldwide AI spending to reach about $2.7 trillion in 2026 and climb to roughly $3.6 trillion in 2027.

CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD), Snowflake (NYSE: SNOW), and Dell Technologies (NYSE: DELL) are competitively positioned to capitalize on that opportunity. While the S&P 500 has returned 13% year to date, these stocks have delivered far superior returns. Here's why they are still worth buying and holding for 10 years.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

CrowdStrike

CrowdStrike's Falcon platform protects businesses from cyberattacks across their cloud systems and user accounts, and growing demand for AI-powered security solutions is fueling its momentum. The stock has doubled this year as management called the second quarter its "best quarter" in history, with net new annual recurring revenue accelerating to 51% year-over-year growth in the fiscal second quarter of 2027.

CrowdStrike's edge is its data. Its platform analyzes about 7 trillion events a day. Management says the company has been labeling this data for a decade, providing it with information that competitors don't have. That advantage shows up in a high subscription-adjusted gross profit margin of 81%.

Management sees a lot more growth ahead. CrowdStrike hit $5.2 billion in ARR in fiscal 2026, and expects full-year fiscal 2027 ARR to reach between $6.3 billion and $6.6 billion. Management now expects to hit its long-term targets one year ahead of schedule, reaching $10 billion in ARR by fiscal 2030 and $20 billion by fiscal 2035.

The stock trades at about 40 times this fiscal year's expected revenue. That's a steep premium, but it reflects a highly profitable business that saw accelerating net new ARR last quarter and a path to more than tripling its ARR over the next decade.

Image source: Getty Images.
Snowflake

Snowflake runs a cloud platform where companies store and analyze their data and build AI applications on top of it. The stock is up about 46% this year as product revenue growth accelerated for the third straight quarter, reaching 37% year over year in the latest quarter (ended July 31).

Companies using Snowflake can pull all their data into one place and control who can access it. This makes it easier for companies to build and run AI agents. The platform is not easy to build, and that edge supports strong profitability, with Snowflake earning a high adjusted gross profit margin of 75%.

GM
F
NVDA

Investors might know General Motors (NYSE: GM) as an automotive giant hailing from Detroit, but the company could also be confused with a magic show with the way GM is making its shares disappear. General Motors has spent tens of billions on share repurchases that have significantly reduced its shares outstanding, in turn boosting earnings per share. Let's take a look at just how much GM has repurchased in recent years, and why investors might want to pay attention to what happens next.

Disappearing act

Below you can see just how impressive GM's share-disappearing act has been, particularly since 2023.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Data source: General Motors' Q3 earnings presentation. Graphic created by author with use of ChatGPT.

If that graphic wasn't compelling enough, consider this: Since the beginning of 2023, GM has reduced its shares outstanding from roughly 1.395 billion down to 849 million as of the third quarter -- a near 40% reduction.

While share buybacks don't guarantee a higher stock price, reducing the share count gives existing investors a larger ownership stake in the business and can help bolster earnings per share, potentially making the stock more attractive. It's not a coincidence that since the beginning of 2023 GM's stock price has soared almost 130%, which is even more meaningful when you compare it to rivals Ford Motor Company (NYSE: F) and Stellantis (NYSE: STLA).

GM data by YCharts

For GM's next trick

Investors tuning into General Motors' third-quarter report may have been surprised at the size of the new multiyear $20 billion share repurchase authorization. Let's take that a step further and do a very basic and simple exercise: Assume that General Motors' earnings will remain flat and the $20 billion will be spent repurchasing shares at an average of $80 per share.

That has the potential to reduce its current 849 million shares outstanding down to a hypothetical 599 million shares. If you do the math, that 29.4% reduction in shares could, in this basic exercise, increase earnings per share by 41.7%. To be clear, this is hypothetical potential and not a forecast, as markets, financials, or other things could change, or GM could find better ways to invest its excess cash flow for higher returns.

Image source: Getty Images.

To be fair, announcing a massive $20 billion share repurchase program is one thing, and generating the cash flow to execute it is another. The good news is that General Motors is practically printing money in large part thanks to lucrative and high-volume sales of its full-size trucks, as well as keeping incentives below the industry average. GM generated $5.9 billion in adjusted automotive free cash flow during the third quarter and ended the period with just over $23 billion in cash and cash equivalents. Further, management also raised its full-year 2026 adjusted automotive free cash flow guidance from a range of $9.5 billion-$11.5 billion to a range of $11.5 billion-$12.5 billion.

title: Is It Too Late to Buy Energy Transfer After a 25% Rally? History Has a Clear Answer.
detail:
Is It Too Late to Buy Energy Transfer After a 25% Rally? History Has a Clear Answer.
Todd Shriber, The Motley Fool
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 11:25 AM PDT 4 min read
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Whether it's cases of fear of missing out (FOMO), strong conviction in specific stocks or sectors, or just good old-fashioned commitment to long-term investing, many of today's retail investors aren't spooked about stocks after significant rallies.

That's relevant in discussing Energy Transfer LP (TXSE: ET), a beloved high-dividend pipeline stock that's surged 25% year to date. With a dividend yield of 6.7%, Energy Transfer is undoubtedly tempting to a broad swath of equity income investors. Still, some may rightly be wondering if they're late to the party given the stock's scorching hot run this year.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Energy Transfer stock is hot, but that's not a reason to avoid it. Image source: Getty Images.

There's no surefire way to know what the future has in store for Energy Transfer, and that's true of any stock. Marty McFly can't fire up the DeLorean and tell us how this energy stock will shape next week, next month, or in 2027. However, Energy Transfer's post-rally history may be instructive.

A run, then a rest

Stocks don't move up in straight lines. Many take breathers following extended rallies. That's been the case with Energy Transfer this year. The war in Iran sent energy prices and equities soaring in the first quarter, and Energy Transfer participated in the fun, notching a mostly smooth move higher.

Those good times extended into the second quarter, a period in which Energy Transfer experienced pullbacks in consecutive months. Still, all those modest dips were bought, and the stock continued to grind higher. That recent history is pertinent today because as of Wednesday, Oct. 21, this pipeline stock retreated 7.8% from its 52-week high.

Investors eyeballing Energy Transfer today should keep a couple of points in mind. First, a decline of 7.8% from a recent high isn't even a correction (that'd be a 10% drop), let alone a full-fledged bear market. Second, when strongly trending stocks pull back, those retreats can range from 5% to 15% and still be considered "healthy" or "normal."

Shares of Energy Transfer are up 185.1% over the past five years, confirming strength. Not only that, but over that period, the stock trounced the Alerian MLP Infrastructure Index, of which it's a member, and all of its dips proved to be buying opportunities.

The dividend buffer

With Energy Transfer, the big source of allure is income. Its 6.7% dividend yield easily tops the 10-year Treasury yield, and, through small but steady increases, the payout has grown in recent years.

SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) could be preparing to shake up the U.S. wireless industry. The company reportedly wants to build a nationwide mobile network to compete with established wireless carriers. While that could be bad news for legacy mobile carriers, it could create a tremendous opportunity for two dividend-paying real estate investment trusts (REITs) that own cell towers: Crown Castle (NYSE:CCI) and American Tower (NYSE:AMT).

Here's a look at the SpaceX rumors and which infrastructure REIT to buy if they prove to be true.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

SpaceX could supercharge demand for cell towers

Earlier this month, SpaceX agreed to purchase a low-band spectrum portfolio from private equity firm Grain Management for $8 billion. This spectrum improves range and allows signals to penetrate through walls and tree cover. It put the company a step closer to launching a mobile service in the U.S.

Now, the company is reportedly taking another step toward that strategy by seeking to secure space on telecom towers. According to a Bloomberg report, SpaceX is looking for access to 80,000 cell tower sites in the U.S. That report noted it's in talks with Crown Castle about space on its tower network. The REIT currently owns, operates, and leases about 40,000 sites across the U.S. American Tower is also a leading tower owner with 42,000 sites across the U.S. and Canada (and more than 106,000 properties in other international markets).

The REITs lease space on those towers to the country's three national mobile carriers (Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile) and other customers. Adding a fourth national carrier would create a new source of demand for space on existing towers. That's noteworthy because tower economics significantly improve with each additional tenant. Due to the high fixed costs of building a tower, the return on investment for a single-tenant lease is low, but increases exponentially with each additional tenant. For example, a sample tower economics model in an American Tower investor presentation shows a 3% return on investment for a single tenant, 13% for two tenants, and 24% for three tenants.

However, there's no guarantee that SpaceX will sign definitive leasing agreements. According to an estimate by TD Cowen, it would cost more than $80 billion to build out a nationwide network. That's a massive capital outlay for a company that's already spending heavily on AI and space. It could partner with an existing carrier, such as T-Mobile.
